title: SID-2 Technical Report: Scaling Search Swarms
summary: SID-2 trains search models with RL to be steered to an objective and an effort, and SID-2 Swarm trains them to search in parallel and share discoveries, so coordinated groups of small models outperform larger individual models. This report covers metric steering, reasoning effort, self-play data, the swarm harness and infrastructure.
body_markdown:
SID-2 is a family of search models trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning. A single model is steered at inference time to the retrieval objective an application needs (NDCG, F1 or Recall@k) and to one of three reasoning efforts, each trained against its own latency budget under an analytic latency model. SID-2 Swarm trains the same models to search in parallel contexts and share what they find, so that coordinated groups of small models outperform larger individual models. This report describes metric steering, reasoning effort, self-play data, the swarm harness and its training, and the infrastructure behind them.

## Introduction


Artificial Intelligence is producing more words per day than human beings write and speak, growing 9–15× year-over-year.1 1


[Ramp AI Index](https://ramp.com/data/ai-index?metric=token-volume&detail=maker&mode=volume) (Kharazian, 2026). Token-volume series, accessed 26 Oct 2026.


We estimate that, as of November 2026, LLMs are generating as many output tokens as exist on the entire public internet every 15 days. As token costs fall2 2


[The plunging price of thought](https://epoch.ai/publications/the-plunging-price-of-thought) (Emberson, Roodman, 2026)


and agent swarms increasingly decouple token generation from human prompting,3 3


[On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/) (OpenAI, 2026)


4 4


[Sharing AI progress in mathematics](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/) (OpenAI, 2026)


we expect this growth to accelerate further. Yet, as with the internet and academic literature, the value of this growing body of information largely hinges on our ability to retrieve it effectively.


As corpora grow, finding relevant evidence becomes harder. Fixed search pipelines built around BM25, embeddings, and rerankers allocate a fixed amount of compute per query, limiting their ability to adapt to query difficulty and corpus size. Predictably, we observe linear degradation of search quality as a function of corpus size. To improve coverage across corpora of varying sizes and complexities, engineers often add query rewrites, routing rules, and specialized processing. These piecemeal fixes create burdensome complexity and, in some cases, they can undermine each other.


SID-1 introduced a new search paradigm that replaced hand-written rules with a more flexible, agentic approach learned through reinforcement learning. It makes an initial search, reads the results, and adapts its search strategy as needed. By dynamically varying the number of turns, SID-1 scales inference-time compute alongside query difficulty, improving retrieval across legal, finance, science, and general knowledge domains.5 5


[SID-1 Technical Report: Test-Time Compute for Retrieval](https://www.sid.ai/research/sid-1-technical-report) (SID, 2025)


Most of the gains come from performance on complex, multi-hop queries where fixed pipelines tend to return only part of the answer. By replacing fixed retrieval pipelines with an agentic approach, we observe substantially less NDCG degradation as corpus size increases (Figure 2).


**Figure 2:** Recall against corpus size (items, logarithmic scale) for SID-2, BM25 @10 and embedding search @10. Each line is a linear fit to the per-corpus points; the ticks over the plot mark reference corpus sizes. The points are read off the draft’s figure and are approximate.


While SID-1’s NDCG degraded more slowly with corpus size than that of fixed pipelines, its scalability remained constrained by latency and its effective context window. Additional turns add latency and accumulate observations in the same context window, effectively capping the volume of evidence that the model can examine. We therefore hypothesized that search would benefit more from division of agentic labor than other domains, such as math and coding. While many other tasks require sequential reasoning over intermediate results, a corpus can be easily divided across agents and searched in parallel. SID-1 demonstrated gains from combining four independent searches and identified coordination as a priority for future work.


SID-2 uses agent swarms to coordinate parallelized searches. Through reinforcement learning, the agents learn to explore in separate contexts and share discoveries that inform subsequent searches. This expands the breadth of evidence examined beyond one agent’s effective context window, while allowing searches to fan out concurrently. In our evaluations, coordinated groups of small models outperform larger, more capable individual models, including in reasoning-heavy domains like legal and finance. The Bitter Lesson6 6


[The Bitter Lesson](http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html) (Sutton, 2019)


does not necessarily call for larger models, but rather methods that scale effectively with compute.


Of course, broader exploration consumes additional compute and may return more evidence than a given use case requires. We therefore train SID-2 for configurable reasoning effort and Metric Steering, allowing users to control the tradeoff between quality and latency and specify their retrieval objective. We improve data, rewards, and model architecture to increase efficiency. At its lowest effort setting, SID-2 outperforms four parallel SID-1 runs using 13× fewer FLOPs per task.


Part of the success of coding agents stems from their ability to complete long-running tasks autonomously. They can inspect a repository, read relevant files, and continue working without waiting for a human to assemble the necessary context. We believe that knowledge work agents in other domains have yet to achieve the same degree of self-sufficiency in part because they face larger and less structured search spaces. SID-2 seeks to address this.


## Capabilities


In service of raw retrieval performance and new use cases we discovered in deployment of SID-1, we train a number of new *capabilities* into SID-2: new ways in which the model can be adapted and scaled in deployment.


**Agent swarms .** For best-in-class retrieval performance, we train SID-2 Swarm, whereby multiple agents can message each other and fork their context into more agents. We find this to be a very promising direction for the problem of search specifically.


**Very low latency settings .** We train SID-2 to have an extremely low reasoning effort mode, while achieving comparable performance to models with 1–2 orders of magnitude more parameters on high reasoning settings.


**Long context.** SID-2 supports a 262k-token context window, and we train on long-context retrieval tasks in our high reasoning effort settings.


**Metric Steering .** We allow users to steer the breadth vs depth tradeoff in the documents returned by SID-2 and SID-2 Swarm by natively training the model to be steerable to different points on the precision-recall curve.


**Complex, multi-corpus environments .** We dedicate significant effort to creating training environments with complex, interlinked corpora with different search tool configurations and filters, based on our insights from deploying SID-1.


## SID-2


### Metric Steering


Part of what makes search challenging is that different applications call for different degrees of depth and breadth. For example, a paralegal reviewing discovery files would prioritize recall (comprehensiveness) over precision, because, in this case, missing a critical piece of evidence is more costly than skimming an extraneous document. By contrast, an e-commerce shopper searching for a ‘40W incandescent lightbulb’ is unlikely to scroll past the first handful of results and therefore values precision more highly. These two users have opposing priorities but are likely given similar tools and see similar results today, depending on corpus sizes. This is because classical search tools like BM25, embeddings, and even SID-1, provide little latitude to hone the recall/precision tradeoff. Rerankers, query rewriters and other techniques can help mitigate this problem, but they do not address the underlying cause.


We therefore introduce *Metric Steering* during post-training, which allows users to specify their primary retrieval objective and steer the model to optimize for it directly within the search loop. SID-2 learns to adapt its search strategy, context management, and reporting behavior to the desired reward metric at inference time. It can natively optimize for the following metrics:


- **NDCG.** Comprehensive search that does not penalize reporting additional background documents (examples: legal, financial or scientific research, compliance).
- **F1.** High-precision, penalizes reporting non-critical documents (examples: job search, customer support, e-commerce).

### Reasoning effort


Like the Federal Reserve, SID-2 has a dual mandate with competing objectives: search quality and speed. The behaviors that improve quality (more searches, more reads, more reasoning, more turns) also tend to increase latency. One of our goals with SID-2 is to give users greater control over where they land on the quality/latency frontier. For some retrieval tasks, such as e-commerce search or doc retrieval for live chat, a slow answer is tantamount to a wrong answer. In other domains, such as legal or scientific research, users may gladly invest additional seconds in exchange for higher-quality results.


**Prior approaches.** Configurable reasoning effort is an obvious way to offer this flexibility and has become standard across many recent models. Implementations take several forms, including binary switches (reasoning on or off), token budgets, and discrete effort levels. DeepSeek trains separate effort specialists, each with its own context window and length penalty.7 7


*DeepSeek-V4 Technical Report* (DeepSeek-AI, 2026)


Moonshot AI uses per-task token budgets during RL for Kimi K3.8 8


*Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence* (Kimi Team, 2026)


NVIDIA introduces a medium-effort mode during SFT and further optimizes it in post-training.9 9


*NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra Technical Report* (NVIDIA, 2026)


Cognition offers a notably explicit approach: SWE-2 subtracts a linear cost penalty from the reward, multiplied by a per-effort coefficient matched to the local slope of the base model’s Pareto frontier.10 10


*Introducing SWE-2: Pushing the Pareto Frontier* (Cognition, 2026)


Despite the growing predominance of configurable reasoning effort, the literature offers surprisingly little guidance on how to train this behavior into a model. Our goal with SID-2 is to support three effort levels: low, medium, and high. We describe our approach in detail to shed light on how it can be done.


**Two-stage training.** Initially, we applied latency pressure from the start of training, but this was overly punitive for a model that had not yet learned how to search effectively. It discouraged exploration of valuable (but time-consuming) search strategies that were necessary to achieve maximum quality. A process must be learned before it can be accelerated, so we train SID-2 in two stages. In the first stage, we ignore latency and reward retrieval quality exclusively, allowing the model to experiment wildly, free of latency constraints. In the second stage, once we observe robust search quality, we add a latency penalty, estimated by the *Latency Model* . This pushes the model to shed latency-inducing behaviors that yield little or no quality improvement.

### Latency model


Token counts, which most prior work either budgets or penalizes, are a poor proxy for agentic search latency. All retrieval calls in a turn share a single backend round, prefill tokens are far cheaper than decoded ones, and later turns decode more slowly as the KV cache grows.


Similarly, wall-clock time during post-training is another flawed latency metric, because it is confounded by how an episode happened to be batched and scheduled on the training cluster and is not necessarily indicative of how it would run in production. Two identical episodes could therefore receive different rewards by virtue of scheduling and concurrency.


Instead, we estimate latency analytically, by replaying each episode as a sequence of forward passes that a production server would run. We price each pass on a target serving GPU and add estimated retrieval backend latency. The result is a deterministic latency estimate for each episode, so the reward only changes if the model’s behavior changes.

### Proposer-solver self-play


Scaling RL on LLMs is limited by compute, training stability, and the availability of appropriately difficult tasks with known solutions. Search is a uniquely attractive candidate for eliminating the third bottleneck, because every task is a query that can be answered by searching a corpus, and a sufficiently large corpus provides a practically limitless supply of potential answers. SID-2 is our first model that moves in this direction. Specifically, we let it propose queries that it then attempts to answer by searching the corpus. Proposer episodes are rewarded for queries that provide useful training signal, whereas solver episodes are rewarded with our standard search rewards.


While proposer/solver episodes do not comprise all of our training data, they do confer several desirable properties even at this scale:


1. **Data-free scaling.** We can improve search performance on any corpus without the need to manually generate or buy additional queries.
2. **Less jaggedness.** Despite performing well on harder queries, SID-1 occasionally struggled with simpler ones. The classic solution to this “jaggedness” is adding easy queries to the training mix. However, doing so indiscriminately creates groups where every attempt in the group scores perfectly, so every advantage is zero and the group contributes no training signal. Oversampling can mitigate this, but it cannot resolve it entirely.15 15


[DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/a4277440d50f1f15d2cb4c14f7e0c0d2-Paper-Conference.pdf) (Yu et al., 2025)


In proposer/solver training, the model is incentivized to exploit these regressions as they appear, creating an online curriculum.


Because the proposer and the solver share weights, our early attempts suffered from “subliminal” communication, in which the model proposed a query paired with a seemingly unrelated set of golden documents, but the solver inexplicably found many of these spurious documents. ### Harness


SID-2 is trained with multi-turn RL in a retrieval harness. During each episode, it searches at least one corpus, reads documents, and reports a ranked list of document IDs once it has enough context to answer the query or is confident that sufficient context does not exist. Each search result and each passage read lands in the model’s context window. Because context is limited and additional context increases latency, we designed the harness to teach SID-2 to manage its context efficiently without sacrificing result quality: SID-2 decides how much text it sees and never sees the same text twice. This allows SID-2 to search documents of arbitrary length and corpora of arbitrary size.


Search results fed back to SID-2 contain only a relevant snippet from each document. The model only reads a document in its entirety when it judges that doing so would be helpful, and as a result uses the read tool infrequently. To select each snippet, we slide a fixed-size window over the document, score each position against the query with BM25 over unigrams and bigrams, and return only the highest-scoring window. The model controls both the number of snippets returned (` limit` ) and the size of each snippet (` snippet_size` ). Neither is directly rewarded or penalized; more and larger snippets cost the model only through the latency terms of the reward. The model can use the read tool to expand the current snippet, or request a larger snippet on the next search.


A potential risk with iterative search is context pollution from redundant reads, particularly when refined queries return overlapping results. To prevent this, each snippet carries a reference` id#start:end` that denotes the character range shown. The harness caches every document surfaced in an episode and keeps track of the character ranges that the model has already seen. If a subsequent search returns redundant text, the redundant range is replaced with a marker, such as` \[seen: "#120:480"\]` . Reads are served from the cache and require no additional round trip to the backend. The model also never sees database IDs. Instead, each document receives a new ID when it first appears in an episode, preventing the policy from memorizing document IDs across epochs.


The same policy must serve real-world deployments that differ in corpus type, search backend and retrieval objective. To ensure that SID-2 generalizes, we vary all three during training. First, we train on a wide range of corpora spanning science, medicine, finance, email, law, web, customer support and structured records. Some environments include more than one of these corpus types, each exposed through its own prefixed tools. Second, we vary tool availability both across and within corpora, because we expect some SID-2 deployments to have only a lexical or only a semantic index, while others will have both. ### Data


In SID-1, we found that public benchmarks such as HotpotQA19 19


[HotpotQA: A Dataset for Diverse, Explainable Multi-hop Question Answering](https://aclanthology.org/D18-1259/) (Yang et al., 2018)

- **Multi-corpus.** Relevant documents are spread across several corpora. The model must decide where to search and combine results across collections.
- **Filtered.** Queries include constraints, such as inclusions and exclusions, that map to metadata filters on the corpus.
- **Tabular data.** The information needed to answer a query is stored in table rows, requiring the model to interpret fields and relationships between them.
- **Findall.** Queries ask for every document satisfying a set of constraints, for example every contract containing a given clause. These tasks require the model to keep searching after finding a relevant document and decide when the result set is complete.


We specifically remove riddle-like questions. Riddle questions are superficially attractive, because they are difficult and provide the intra-group reward differences required for group-relative training. This makes them common in search benchmarks and synthetic datasets, for example Browsecomp-Plus.


But riddle-like questions are not realistic: Outside of game shows, few people ask unnecessarily obfuscated queries. For example, riddle-like questions replace common terms with indirect descriptions and/or rare synonyms (the “18000 island nation” instead of “Indonesia”). We believe that optimizing puzzle solving skews performance away from the searches people and agents actually perform. One particular such example is Browsecomp-Plus.

### Search parallelizes well


Search is a divisible task. Recently, Ord27 27


[Swarm scaling](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/6cb7qd3RSkgnviCpf/swarm-scaling) (Ord, 2026)


found that web search was much more parallelizable than other tasks for agent swarms. Specifically, a 2× increase in parallel tokens yielded similar performance to an ≈ 1.72× increase in sequential tokens for web search, in comparison to an ≈ 1.48× increase in finding software vulnerabilities and an ≈ 1.39× increase in general terminal tasks.


Search algorithms have a tradeoff between breadth (inspecting many items) and depth (inspecting each item more deeply). We hypothesize that for many natural language search use cases there is a high proposer-verifier gap, so that scaling depth saturates early, meaning that scaling breadth is often more advantageous.


In the case of agentic search, the breadth vs. depth tradeoff manifests as a design choice between using many small models in parallel (which will look at more documents) or a single large model (which will expend more FLOPs per document). Provided a document, determining whether it answers a query is usually straightforward, so we hypothesize that swarms of small models will beat fewer, larger models on most search tasks.


Scaling to parallel agents also has attractive properties for decreasing latency: While single-agent generation is bounded by the tokens per second per user (i.e., interactivity), multiple agents can be scaled arbitrarily using concurrent generation within and between replicas. Further, within a deployed replica, forking agents on a shared prefix can ease total memory28 28

### Multi-agent harness design


Our initial experiments in this direction used a harness with separate roles of *stem* and *fork* agents. *Stem* agents could only call a` fork` tool, which would spawn *fork* agents that share their context with the stem. *Fork* agents can search and push helpful documents back to the stem. This harness was hand-designed to induce a large amount of KV-cache re-use and minimize context pollution for the stem.


Unfortunately, we observed models would (1) persistently be confused as to their role and try to call tools that aren’t available to them and (2) the stem model would have a hard time understanding how the search tools would behave (as it could no longer learn this in-context).


We gradually relaxed the harness we used, eventually converging on a harness similar to OpenAI’s multi-agent harness.25 25


In this harness, every agent can call:


- the search tools;
- ` fork` : spawns new agents with specified names and forked context (the maximum number of agents is capped globally);
- ` message` : sends a textual message to a list of agents’ inboxes;
- ` wait` : waits until a message arrives in this agent’s inbox;
- ` list` : lists all the agents and their status;
- ` report_helpful_ids` : ends the calling agent’s part of the episode and reports its most helpful documents by passing their identifiers.


Messages in a given agent’s inbox are appended to the result of its next tool call. If a message is not delivered (because, for example, the recipient has already reported), the sender receives textual feedback. At the end of the episode, all the documents reported across` report_helpful_ids` calls are fused with RRF.


For both harnesses, we compute the score of the whole episode at its end and apply the resulting advantage evenly to all agents in the episode. By viewing the other agents’ messages as observations from the RL environment, we can see that the standard policy gradient theorem generalizes to this multi-agent setting.


### Simulated-latency request scheduling for high-throughput multi-agent RL


To maximize throughput during RL training, generations are generally configured to be asynchronously scheduled by environments. For our single-agent setup, the wall-clock time at which requests are scheduled does not affect the environment observations or reward, and so does not materially affect the training process. However, for multi-agent training, scheduling affects the order in which messages from other agents arrive, letting agents become arbitrarily out of sync with one another. This can become particularly egregious when agents in the same episode are routed to different rollout engines, some of which can have a long request queue. As deployment is configured for lower throughput to decrease latency, we expect agents to be largely in sync, creating a mismatch between the behavior we encourage in training and the one we desire in deployment. We illustrate this effect in Figure 9.


To remedy this, we leverage our *Latency Model* to attach a simulated latency to every completion and message. If one agent is more than two seconds of simulated latency ahead of others then the harness will wait for other agents to catch up before scheduling its next turn. Likewise, a message whose simulated send time is ahead of its recipient’s clock is held back until the recipient catches up.

### Training optimizations


We dedicate significant effort to increasing our training pipeline throughput. We use a fully asynchronous training pipeline using PipelineRL36 36

with an EAGLE draft head for rollout;37 37

Leveraging roofline throughput estimates assuming good memory bandwidth and FLOPs utilization, we carefully analyze cross-device communication bottlenecks to configure expert, tensor, data and context parallelism. We also control how many episodes are scheduled in parallel to mitigate re-prefilling tokens during rollout. In total, these optimizations compounded to achieve a 6× boost in training throughput over a naive approach using SLIME’s default implementation.


### Train-inference mismatch


We take care to mitigate two types of mismatch throughout training, rollout and deployment: (1) tokenization mismatches5 5


that cause catastrophic collapse of models during training and invalidate the KV cache in deployment, increasing costs and latency, and (2) numerical mismatches between training and inference that degrade performance.38 38


[Your Efficient RL Framework Secretly Brings You Off-Policy RL Training](https://fengyao.notion.site/off-policy-rl) (Yao et al., 2025)

#### Responses API for eliminating tokenization mismatches


To avoid tokenization mismatches, we design our training framework to be fully Tokens-In/Tokens-Out (TI/TO). This completely eliminates tokenization mismatches during RL runs,5 5


but naively means that RL environments must be written in tokens, presenting difficulties when evaluating models with different tokenizers or that are only available via API. To respect TI/TO while writing environments in a messages-based format, we base our training infrastructure on the Responses API40 40


[New tools for building agents](https://openai.com/index/new-tools-for-building-agents/) (OpenAI, 2025)


via a *Responses Translation Layer* , which we keep separate from the rollout engine. During an RL run, in` store=true` mode this translation layer presents a Responses-compatible endpoint to the environments, but it also stores the exact input and output tokens in a given turn and chains turns together with the` previous_response_id` parameter. For multi-agent training (seeSID-2 Swarm ), the` previous_response_id` s form a tree. For each new request during training, the translation layer reconstructs the exact chain of preceding tokens via tracing this tree, renders the new message in tokens and parses the model response back to a message. When an episode is finished, this chain of tokens is extracted and passed to the training engine.


To respect Zero Data Retention (ZDR) during deployment, the Responses Translation Layer encrypts the preceding tokens and sends them to the user; in the next turn, the user returns these encrypted tokens with the new message.
